html:
The Faras cathedral murals are some 120 Christian wall paintings from the cathedral of Faras in Lower Nubia, painted between the 8th and 14th centuries. They were rescued in the 1960s, just before the waters of Lake Nasser drowned the site.

Faras had been the capital of Nobadia, which turned Christian in the 6th century and later joined Makuria. The cathedral was rebuilt in 707 by Bishop Paulos, and over the centuries its walls were painted again and again with saints, angels, the Virgin and Child, bishops and Nubian kings. The style draws on Byzantine and Coptic art, but the faces and dress show Nubian ways. Sand later buried the building, which kept the paintings safe.

When the Aswan High Dam was built, a Polish team led by Kazimierz Michałowski dug the cathedral out and cut the paintings off the walls. Half are now in the National Museum in Warsaw and half in the Sudan National Museum in Khartoum.
